dataset.name: Soil Carbon Dynamics Following Land Use Changes and Conversion to Oil Palm Plantations in Tropical Lowlands Inferred From Radiocarbon
description: We measured the 14C and 13C isotopic values of soil organic carbon in mineral soil from lowland tropical forests to provide insight into how quickly carbon is turning over in the soil following conversion of primary forests to oil palm plantations. In addition to areas converted to oil palm plantations in Peru, Indonesia, and Cameroon, we examine pastures and secondary forests in Peru as a comparison to the carbon cycling processes operating in the oil palm plantations.

This dataset includes radiocarbon (Δ14C) and stable carbon (δ13C) isotopes of soil organic carbon in mineral soils from natural lowland forests and oil palm plantations in Peru, Indonesia, and Cameroon. We additionally examine plots of secondary forests following agricultural use and pastures on cleared natural forest in Peru. In addition to isotopic data, this dataset includes soil carbon and nitrogen concentrations and stock, soil texture (percent sand, silt, and clay), pH, ECEC (effective cation exchange capacity), base saturation, and bulk density. Soils were sampled in 4 depth increments to 100 cm depth.
This dataset supports the publication Finstad et al., 2020.

Finstad, K., van Straaten, O., Veldkamp, E., & McFarlane, K. (2020). Soil carbon dynamics following land use changes and conversion to oil palm plantations in tropical lowlands inferred from radiocarbon. Global Biogeochemical Cycles, 34, e2019GB006461. https://doi.org/10.1029/2019GB006461

measurementTechnique:
Methods are described in detail in Finstad et al., 2020.
Finstad, K., van Straaten, O., Veldkamp, E., & McFarlane, K. (2020). Soil carbon dynamics following land use changes and conversion to oil palm plantations in tropical lowlands inferred from radiocarbon. Global Biogeochemical Cycles, 34, e2019GB006461. https://doi.org/10.1029/2019GB006461

We examined the impact of converting natural forests to oil palm plantations, pastures, and the subsequent regeneration of secondary forests in lowland tropical forests in three regions across the world that are heavily impacted by land use changes. Within each region, two to six reference plots in natural forests were selected with characteristics as representative of the regional soil characteristics as possible (van Straaten et al., 2015). A paired land use plot (oil palm plantation, pasture, or secondary forest) was then selected adjacent to the reference plot. We attempted to match as closely as possible climate, landscape position, soil texture, and soil color between paired sites. This allowed us to compare reference plots to the land use plots and attribute changes seen in the soil carbon dynamics to the land management. All three study regions are situated on Acrisols or Ferralsols and are characterized by low soil pH, low cation exchange capacity, and low base saturation.
The sites in Peru were established west of the city of Pucallpa in the Ucayali Region, which is located in the Amazonian basin. Six natural forest plots, four oil palm plantations, three pastures, and four secondary forests were selected. The oil palm plantations were converted from pastures between 10 and 20 years ago, and the pasture sites were converted from natural forests between 10 and 14 years ago. The secondary forests had previously been used for agriculture and were restored to forests between 9 and 17 years ago. In Indonesia, the paired plots were established in the Jambi province on the island of Sumatra using four reference plots and four corresponding oil palm plantations converted between 10 and 19 years ago. Two references plots were established in Cameroon along with three oil palm plantations east and south of the capital Yaoundé. The oil palm plantations in Cameroon ranged in age from 10 to 15 years.
All of the selected oil palm sites were established by small holder farmers who do not have access to heavy equipment. During site selection, we purposefully excluded sites where mechanized clearing methods were used (i.e., bulldozers). In Peru, the oil palm sites were originally cleared using hand tools, such as chainsaws, for pastures. After a period of time, the sites were converted to oil palm plantations (Table 1). Cattle grazing resulted in significantly higher bulk densities in these sites than the original forests. In Cameroon and Indonesia, natural forests were manually cleared using chainsaws, and then the fallen debris was burnt. Immediately thereafter, the sites were used for agriculture (rice, maize, yams, and groundnuts) for 1–2 years, whereupon oil palm was planted. At these sites, there were no significant differences in the bulk density between the original forest and the oil palm.
van Straaten, O., Corre, M. D., Wolf, K., Tchienkoua, M., Cuellar, E., Matthews, R. B., & Veldkamp, E. (2015). Conversion of lowland tropical forests to tree cash crop plantations loses up to one-half of stored soil organic carbon. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 112(32), 9956–9960. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1504628112

A soil pit was dug at each site and soil samples collected at depth intervals of 0–10, 10–30, 30–50, and 50–100 cm. δ13C analysis of bulk soils and roots <2 mm were measured by an isotope ratio mass spectrometer interfaced to an elemental analyzer at the Center for Stable Isotope Research and Analysis at the Georg-August University of Goettingen, Germany. Bulk density was measured in each pit at 10, 20, 40, 75, and 100 cm on soil that was dried at 105°C for 48 hr. Total organic carbon (TOC) and total nitrogen (TN) were determined using a CN analyzer (CN Elementar Analyzer Vario EL) at the Georg-August University of Goettingen, Germany, on soil that was air-dried, 2 mm sieved, and ground. Carbon and nitrogen stocks were calculated from bulk density measurements and TOC or TN. Changes in bulk density caused by different land uses can have a profound influence on SOC stock comparisons. To account for this and achieve accurate estimates, the bulk density of the reference plot was used for SOC stock determination in the converted plots. This approach ensures that SOC stocks are not overestimated at the converted sites due to differences in bulk density stemming from land use changes.
Further analyses of chemical and physical characteristics were performed on surface (0–10 cm) and depth (50–100 cm) samples. This included soil particle size via the pipette method, pH, effective cation exchange capacity (ECEC), and base saturation. Soil pH was determined on air-dried, 2-mm sieved samples using a soil to water ratio of 1:4. ECEC was measured by mixing an unbuffered 1 M NH4Cl solution with air-dried, 2-mm sieved samples. The supernatant was analyzed for the concentration of Ca, Mg, K, Na, Fe, Al, and Mn on an inductively coupled plasma-atomic emission spectrometer (Spectroflame; Spectro Analytical Instruments). Base saturation was calculated from the ECEC data and is reported as a percent.
Radiocarbon analyses were performed at the Center for Accelerator Mass Spectrometry at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in Livermore, California, on the Van de Graaf FN accelerator mass spectrometer (AMS). Between 10 and 250 mg of air-dried, 2-mm sieved, and ground soil was weighed into a quartz tube with CuO and Ag and then combusted to CO2 at 900°C. The CO2 was reduced to graphite on iron powder in the presence of H2 at 570°C. The AMS measurements had an average precision of 2.9‰. Measured δ13C values were used to correct for mass-dependent fractionation, and 14C isotope values are reported in the standard Δ14C notation with corrections for 14C decay since 1950 and the year of sampling.
